t: Introduction to the topic and lesson plan
n: In this lesson we study connective tissue dysplasia, CTD for short, and its cardiovascular consequences. CTD is associated with disturbed collagen synthesis. In the heart it may appear as left ventricular false tendons, LVFT. Marfan syndrome arises from a change in the FBN1 gene, and its main cardiovascular sign is dilatation of the aortic root. Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome arises from a mutation of the COL3A1 gene, and rupture of arteries is possible. CTD is a common hereditary pathology, and cardiovascular changes are regarded as one of the causes of sudden death in young people.

t: CTD: definition and prevalence (forensic medical aspect)
n: We consider the definition and prevalence of CTD from the forensic medical point of view. CTD is widespread among the population, even among those who consider themselves healthy. Manifestations range from subclinical changes to severe diseases: Marfan syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. This is a hereditary systemic pathology of the formation of connective tissue structures. Remember: changes in the cardiovascular system are one of the causes of sudden death in young people of working age.

t: External and internal signs of CTD (examination of the corpse)
n: The external and internal signs of CTD are found on examination of the corpse. External signs: asthenic build, tall stature, long limbs and fingers, narrow long chest, protruding or sunken sternum. Also spinal deformities, that is kyphosis, scoliosis, hyperlordosis, and poor development of subcutaneous fat and skeletal muscle. Anomalies of tooth position and varicose dilatation of the superficial veins of the legs also occur. On internal examination, absence of cartilaginous rings in the large bronchi, splanchnoptosis, intestinal diverticulosis and dolichosigmoid are found.

t: Marfan, osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos: clinical picture
n: We compare the clinical picture of Marfan syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. A triad is characteristic of Marfan syndrome: involvement of the musculoskeletal system, cardiovascular system and eyes. In the eye, myopia, lens dislocation and iris hypoplasia are seen. Osteogenesis imperfecta appears first of all as pathological fragility of bones. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is characterised by laxity of ligaments and increased mobility of joints.

t: What is CTD? The basic concept
n: Let us clarify what CTD is. CTD is associated with disturbed collagen synthesis. It is widespread both among the healthy population and among persons with disabilities. Congenital disabilities are mainly of genetic origin and are usually associated with mutations of genes controlling collagen synthesis. In some regions the occurrence of CTD may reach 70–90%, and in the Urals it is especially high. Attention, there is a risk of error: false tendons by themselves are not regarded as a pathological finding, since at rest the function of the heart remains normal.

t: Mechanism of CTD: from collagen to the heart
n: We consider the mechanism of CTD from collagen to the heart. Disturbed collagen synthesis lowers the stiffness of connective tissue. In hollow organs, additional fibres appear. They strengthen like extra beams in a bridge. In the study, 2–5 thick, that is >2 mm, false tendons were found in the left ventricle. The chain is as follows: disturbed collagen synthesis, lowered tissue stiffness, additional fibrous structures, false tendons in the left ventricle and an effect on cardiac reserve.

Left ventricular false tendons, LVFT. CTD is associated with disturbed collagen synthesis. In the heart, mainly in the left ventricle, false tendons appear, keeping the pump function close to normal. Only those LVFT were counted as significant that were thicker than 2 mm, transverse and/or oblique, connecting the interventricular septum with the free wall, mainly in the basal or mid part. In 100% of the participants examined, from 2 to 5, mean 3.4 ± 1, LVFT were found. It did not depend on type of disability, sport, sex or age. Attention: LVFT is not a disease. At rest cardiac function is normal, so LVFT is not a pathological finding, but it is associated with increased mechanical asynchrony.

Quick question: CTD and LVFT. Question: what additional structures appear in the left ventricle of the heart in connective tissue dysplasia? Answer: false tendons, LVFT, left ventricular false tendons. They were regarded as a strong marker of CTD. In the study only thick, >2 mm, transverse and/or oblique tendons were counted. They connect opposite walls of the left ventricle. Modern cardiology does not call LVFT a pathological finding: at rest cardiac function remains within the normal range.

t: Four thanatological syndromes of sudden death in CTD
n: In CTD there are four thanatological syndromes of sudden death. The arrhythmic syndrome, with ventricular fibrillation. The valvular syndrome, dysplasia of the valves: dilatation of fibrous rings, prolapse of leaflets, short and abnormally positioned chordae. The vascular syndrome, anomalies of origin of the coronary arteries, of the pulmonary artery and sinuses of Valsalva, and rupture of a congenital aneurysm of the heart, aorta or cerebral vessels. In the thoracodiaphragmatic syndrome, a small heart rotated about its axis, an aorta that is dilated and of low elasticity, against a background of chest deformity. All of them, by reducing the compensatory capacity of the cardiovascular system, appear with ventricular hypertrophy.

Histological changes in CTD. In the aorta, elastic membranes thin and fragment, and collagen fibres are arranged chaotically. In the thickness of the muscle layer and around the vasa vasorum, overgrowth of connective tissue, haemorrhage into the wall and small cysts are found. At the origin of the branches of the anterior cerebral artery, the muscle layer is atrophic and collagen fibres are disordered. In the heart valves, cells are fewer, collagen fibres more, and myxomatous dystrophy of the connective tissue is seen. In the myocardium there is uneven hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes and diffuse cardiosclerosis.

t: Aortic aneurysm: distinguishing hypertensive medionecrosis from CTD
n: In aortic aneurysm, hypertensive medionecrosis and CTD must be distinguished. Medionecrosis as a complication of hypertension leads to sudden death with a dissecting aneurysm. In histology, foci of breakdown filled with mucoid substance in the media, that is Erdheim cysts, defects of elasticity, rupture and haemorrhage into the wall are seen. Hypertensive medionecrosis must be differentiated from such a complication in CTD syndrome. In diagnosis, the history, external signs and changes in other organs are assessed together. In hypertension these are cardiac hypertrophy and renal changes.

General description of Marfan syndrome. Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant and is regarded as the commonest form of hereditary connective tissue diseases. The classical triad: involvement of the cardiovascular system, eyes and musculoskeletal system. Any organ with a connective tissue component may be involved. The prevalence is about 1 in 5000–10,000 people. If the main organs are not affected, diagnosis is difficult and the figure may be underestimated. There is age-related penetrance: signs appear later, often after 20 years. Therefore diagnosis in children is difficult.

t: The FBN1 gene and function of fibrillin-1
n: The FBN1 gene and function of fibrillin-1. Variants of FBN1, 15q21, are the cause of Marfan syndrome, MFS. The gene consists of 65 exons. The microfibrils of fibrillin-1 control the release and storage of TGFβ, that is growth factor β. The chain is as follows: FBN1 variant, fibrillin-1, 2871 a.a., elastic fibre via the microfibril, regulation of the amount of TGFβ and multi-organ signs. The protein is present in the heart, vessels, eyes, skin, cartilage and lungs, which is why the signs are varied.

The Ghent criteria, 2010. Two cardinal features: dilatation of the aortic root and ectopia lentis, that is displacement of the lens from its place. The systemic score is made up of skeletal and facial features, myopia, mitral valve prolapse, MVP, pneumothorax and dural ectasia. According to the table: if the family history is negative, aortic root Z ≥ 2 and ectopia lentis, FBN1 or a score ≥7 are needed. Family history positive, over 20 years: Z ≥ 2 and Marfan in the family. Family history positive, under 20 years: Z ≥ 3 and Marfan in the family. Attention: if there is Marfan in the family, Z ≥ 3 before age 20, and ≥ 2 in adults. In the 2–3 range, follow-up.

t: Early-onset MFS and the classical form
n: The early-onset form, eoMFS, is more severe than the classical form. In it mitral regurgitation is 89%, tricuspid 62%, and aortic dilatation 96%. Onset is perinatal to the first years, and the cause is heart failure through regurgitation. Family history is often negative, 62–78%. Prognosis is poor, on average 16.3 months. Classical MFS begins in childhood, is age-dependent, aortic dissection or rupture is important, and it is also detected through family screening. The Zarate score: 9 clinical features and FBN1, exons 24–32. If ≥14 points, sensitivity is 100% and specificity 92%. Attention: a variant in exons 24–32 alone is insufficient for the diagnosis of eoMFS, and scoring is obligatory.

Aortic root: Z-score and measurement. In adults absolute diameter is used. In children, because of growth, this is unsuitable, so the Z-score is used. The Z-score shows by how many standard deviations the value differs from the mean, taking account of age, sex, height and weight. In the population a Z-score >2 occurs in 2.3 % and >3 in 0.13 %. According to Ghent 2010, in children Z ≥ 3. Nomograms give different Z-scores, so in one patient use the same method and the same nomogram each time.

t: Rate of aortic dilatation and BAV
n: Rate of aortic dilatation and BAV. In healthy people the aortic root grows by about 0.1 mm per year. In children with MFS on treatment this is 0.5–0.8 mm/year, sometimes reaching 3 mm/year. In adults the rate is slower, 0.3–0.7 mm/year. The fastest growth is seen in men and in patients with a larger root at diagnosis. Bicuspid aortic valve, BAV, is 1–2 % in the general population and about 1.8 % in Marfan syndrome. In MFS patients with BAV, dilatation of the aortic root is commoner. In BAV aortopathy the ascending aorta is more affected. For prophylactic surgery, the largest diameter of the root or ascending aorta is taken.

Quick question: Z-score and Ghent. Question: why is the Z-score threshold in children taken as 3? Answer: in a child a small difference in measurement changes the Z-score sharply. Mean dilatation in early childhood may later disappear. There is as yet no multicentre study comparing the thresholds >2 and >3 for children. At a Z-score of 2–3, children without clinical signs need echocardiography every 1–2 years. With a major systemic sign or growth, the threshold falls to >2. Attention, risk of error: >2 and >3 are not the same. According to Ghent 2010, with a family history, the Z-score is ≥3 in those under 20 and ≥2 in adults.

Conservative treatment: β-blocker and ARB. Treatment begins when the diagnosis is made or when dilatation of the aortic root is observed. A β-blocker and an angiotensin receptor blocker, ARB, slow dilatation of the aortic root. Result of Pitcher's meta-analysis: with ARB the growth of the Z-score fell by about half. The effect of a β-blocker is similar to ARB. When ARB and β-blocker were used together, the reduction was at least by half and surgery was delayed. After surgery the drug is continued, since the risk of dissection of the distal aorta remains.

Physical activity and lifestyle. Isometric exercises requiring straining or the Valsalva manoeuvre, contact sports and heavy exercise are avoided, since aortic dilatation may accelerate. Frequent explosive exercises and collision sports are dangerous: they may intensify aortic dilatation and provoke acute dissection. For those who are able, light to moderate aerobic exercise, light recreational sports and light weights with many repetitions without straining are recommended. Most exercise at about 50% of power. Wind instruments at a professional level may affect aortic dilatation through Valsalva. This is a personal observation, and research is needed.

Indications for aortic surgery. When body surface area reaches that of an adult, at 10–12 years, repair of the aortic root and mitral valve is regarded as safer. In valve-sparing surgery, reimplantation is better than remodelling, especially in those over 10. In adults without risk factors, surgery is indicated at a diameter ≥50 mm. If a risk factor is present, the threshold is lower, ≥45 mm. Examples of risk factors: dissection in the family and growth >3 mm/year. There is no single guideline for children. Surgery is carried out in a specialised centre, because complications are frequent and may be multisystem.

Valves: mitral and tricuspid prolapse. Mitral valve prolapse, MVP, occurs in 32–38% of children with Marfan, 40–68% of adults, and 1–2% of the general population. In Marfan the risk of complications with MVP is 28%, in idiopathic MVP 13%. Complications: surgery, endocarditis, heart failure. Tricuspid valve prolapse, TVP, is 68.5% in children, that is 89 of 130, and may be a sign of a more severe phenotype. TVP by age: at 0–10 years 4 %, at 10–20 years 17 %, at 20–30 years 29 %, at 30–40 years 32 %.

Cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. The prevalence of Marfan cardiomyopathy is 3–68%. It involves both ventricles, giving systolic and diastolic disturbance. The cause may be an anomaly of fibrillin-1. Ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias occur even without valve changes. Dangerous arrhythmia 7–9%, sudden cardiac death up to 4%. Corrected QT, QTc, >440 ms occurs in 9–20% of children and 16–20% of adults and does not depend on aortic dilatation. Be careful with QT-prolonging drugs. In assessing risk, ventricular ectopy, ventricular tachycardia, systolic dysfunction and NT-proBNP are taken into account. NT-proBNP is the strongest.

t: Eye and skeletal manifestations in children
n: Eye and skeletal manifestations in children. Lens displacement, ectopia lentis, EL, is 49% in children, that is 25 of 52, of which 68% are bilateral. In adults about 60%. EL is not specific to Marfan. Myopia >3 dioptres in 34.9% of children, in controls 12.9%. The cornea is flattened. Severe myopia is a risk sign for lens displacement. Chest deformity rises from 43% to 62%, scoliosis from 16% to 59%, from 0–6 to 15–17 years. Height is above controls, but is not a criterion. Eye examination is carried out at diagnosis and at least once a year. Measurement of axial length of the eye and corneal curvature is recommended.

t: Case analysis: a child from a Marfan family
n: Case analysis: a child from a Marfan family. Situation: a child examined because a pathogenic FBN1 variant was found in the parents. The genotype is positive, the phenotype so far negative. The aortic root Z-score is between 2 and 3, that is a grey zone. For asymptomatic children, echocardiography every 1–2 years is recommended. Attention: a Z-score >2 and >3 are not the same. In children the diagnostic threshold is 3: a small difference in measurement strongly affects the Z-score, and mild dilatation may later disappear. Question: should lifelong treatment begin now? The source says that pre-emptive lifelong treatment of a child with a normal aorta may not be the best option. The main rule is observation.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vEDS. vEDS is a severe multisystem connective tissue disease caused by a mutation in the COL3A1 gene, the α1 chain of type III collagen, autosomal dominant. The danger: rupture of medium and large arteries, intestine, pregnant uterus, liver and spleen is possible. Aortic rupture in pregnancy is the commonest cause of death in women. Signs: easy bruising, thin transparent skin, visible veins, a characteristic face, spontaneous pneumothorax, early varicose veins and hypermobility of small joints. Gum fragility is also among the other signs.

t: Type III collagen: synthesis and assembly
n: Synthesis and assembly of type III collagen. Three α1(III) chains are encoded by the COL3A1 gene and form a homotrimer. The path is as follows: three proα1(III) chains are synthesised, hydroxylation and folding occur in the endoplasmic reticulum, then the chains assemble in the direction from C to N, forming a triple helix. In the Golgi and the extracellular matrix the propeptide is cleaved. After the propeptides are cleaved, type III collagen forms heterotypic fibrils with type I collagen. Every third residue is glycine, Gly-Xaa-Yaa. Mutations often affect glycine precisely.

COL3A1 mutations and the genotype–phenotype relationship. Glycine substitution, about 65%, and splice-site variants, about 25%, make up the bulk of COL3A1 mutations. In exon-skipping splice-site variants, median survival is the lowest. In null mutations, complications begin two decades later, penetrance is low, and the events are mainly vascular. Attention: substitution of glycine by a large radical, for example arginine or valine, is more severe. A small radical, alanine, serine, cysteine, is milder.

Mouse models of vEDS. The Col3a1−/− mouse has skin wounds, and in the aortic media collagen fibrils are reduced or absent. Col3a1+/− mice live normally, but in the aorta and intestine there is little collagen III and wall strength is reduced. In the Tg-G182S model the skin is thin and the aorta fragile, but there is no rupture. In models with a glycine mutation, G209S and G938D, there is aortic rupture leading to sudden death, G938D being more severe. A mutation closer to the C-terminus is more severe. In the Tsk2/+ mouse, Cys33Ser, the skin is thickened and there is much collagen III, which differs sharply from vEDS.

t: Pathogenesis of vEDS and approaches to treatment
n: Pathogenesis of vEDS and approaches to treatment. The reduction of extracellular collagen III is clear. The role of ER stress is unclear, and whether it is cause or consequence is disputed. The chain: COL3A1 mutation, reduction of collagen III, defect of the extracellular matrix and rise in MMP, activation of PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK, risk of aortic rupture. In mice, blocking the PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway reduced mortality. In pregnancy the oxytocin signal is significant. Celiprolol did not receive FDA approval. MMP inhibitors and gene therapy are still at the research stage.

Experimental therapeutic targets in vEDS. The PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway was identified in two models with a glycine mutation. The action of ruboxistaurin, PKCβ, cobimetinib, MEK, and hydralazine was tested. Protection by hydralazine was lost in puberty, especially in males. Together with spironolactone, mortality was eliminated. Doxycycline, a broad-spectrum MMP inhibitor, reduced aortic changes in Col3a1+/− mice. RNA interference targeting mutant COL3A1 mRNA in patient fibroblasts improved collagen fibril formation. So far all this is only at the research stage.

Case analysis: vEDS and pregnancy. Situation: a pregnant woman with a diagnosis of vEDS. Pregnancy-related aortic rupture is the commonest cause of death in women with vEDS at this age. In mice the PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway was intensified in pregnancy and lactation. An oxytocin receptor antagonist and removal of the pups gave 95% survival. Current treatment is symptomatic: keeping blood pressure normal, ARBs and β-blockers. In mice losartan and propranolol lowered pressure but did not reduce rupture. Question: why may lowering pressure alone be insufficient, and why is the period of lactation regarded as dangerous?

Conclusion and key messages. In CTD, false tendons may occur in the left ventricle of the heart. If function at rest is normal, they are not a disease in themselves. In vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vEDS, a COL3A1 mutation leads to rupture of arteries. In Marfan, FBN1, the aortic root dilates, mitral prolapse and arrhythmia occur, and a β-blocker and ARB are used. From the forensic medical point of view, in CTD sudden death occurs through the arrhythmic, valvular, vascular and thoracodiaphragmatic syndromes.
